issue: Quantitative claim is wrong by a factor of ten. The bullet prints 'extreme sparsity (16/86 ~ 1.8% expert activation)'. 16/86 = 0.18605 = 18.6%, not 1.8%. The printed fraction and the printed percentage are mutually exclusive, and the percentage is load-bearing: the sentence uses it to argue that the memory-bound EP decision is made against total rather than active parameters, and the bullet's closing claim about an 'activated-vs-total residency crossover' rests on the sparsity magnitude.
evidence: Printed p. 181, bullet 2 ('How should EP sizing and all-to-all communication be budgeted for frontier MoE models at extreme sparsity?'). Recomputation: 16 / 86 = 0.1860465; x100 = 18.60%. To yield ~1.8% the denominator must be ~889 (16/896 = 1.786%), which contradicts the '512 experts' printed two clauses earlier. The same bullet prints 'routes 1e1 of 512 experts' - '1e1' is not a well-formed count (10 in scientific notation, or a mangled '16'/'10') - so neither the numerator nor the denominator of the sparsity fraction can be recovered from the page. 'Kimi 10qB' is likewise a malformed parameter count. Note the operator is '~', so the defect is not a rounding quibble: 18.6% vs 1.8% is a factor of 10, far outside any rounding bound.
acceptance_test: Recover the active-expert count, total-expert count and activated/total parameter split from the cited primary sources ([1P] arXiv 2606.24653 / 2607.24653 and the HF model card). Print one self-consistent triple (active / total = percentage) with correct rounding. Delete '1e1' and '10qB' or replace them with well-formed numerals. Then re-derive the sentence: if the corrected sparsity is ~18.6%, the 'extreme sparsity' framing and the 'activated-vs-total residency crossover' argument must be re-argued, not merely re-digitised.

issue: Panel A draws the weight matrix as a single undivided bar with two arrows leaving it, which reads as the same matrix being handed to both GPUs (replication) rather than being partitioned across them (sharding). The panel title says 'splits one layer's weights' and the caption says 'Tensor parallel shards one layer's weight matrix across GPUs', but the drawn object is never divided.
evidence: Printed p. 173, panel A: one blue hatched bar labeled 'one layer's weight matrix W' spanning both GPUs, with two blue arrows descending to 'GPU 0' and 'GPU 1'. The arrows leave from different x positions, which weakly hints at a partition, but no boundary, no shard labels, and no 'W[:, :d/2]' / 'W[:, d/2:]]' annotation is present. acceptance_test: The bar must be visibly partitioned into two labeled shards (e.g. 'W[:, 0:d/2]' and 'W[:, d/2:d]'), each routed to exactly one GPU, with the partition boundary drawn. issue: The body prose identifies replicated activations as a defining property of TP ('activations are replicated'), but the figure shows no activations at all. The only blue element is the weight bar, so the figure depicts TP as a scheme in which only weights move. evidence: Printed p. 173, panel A and the paragraph immediately below the figure: 'Tensor parallel shards one layer's weight matrix across GPUs - activations are replicated, and each GPU's partial sums are all-reduced...'. Acceptance: the figure shows both the replicated input and the reduced output, so the reader can see that TP's per-layer traffic is activation traffic.

figure: FIGURE 11.2 — 'Serving = four separate concerns, not a stack' (2×2 box grid: 1 Request scheduling / 2 State management / 3 Reuse / 4 Resource specialization)
issue: The figure's border-style encoding contradicts the caption's own legend. The caption states: 'the canonical baseline uses the first three, resource specialization joins when the workload outgrows a node (dashed border) — not in the canonical baseline'. That makes dashed border = 'not in the canonical baseline'. But in the rendered figure, boxes 2 (State management) and 3 (Reuse) are ALSO drawn with dashed borders, while box 1 (Request scheduling) is the only solid-bordered box. Under the caption's stated convention, the figure therefore asserts that state management and reuse are excluded from the canonical baseline — the exact opposite of the caption's sentence and of the surrounding chapter (Ch. 11 repeatedly treats PagedAttention and prefix caching as part of the canonical baseline). There is no legend anywhere on the page to disambiguate the border styles, so the reader has no way to resolve the conflict.
evidence: Rendered page 212 (printed 192): box 1 border = solid purple; box 2 = dashed red; box 3 = dashed green; box 4 = dashed orange. Caption text on the same page: 'the canonical baseline uses the first three, resource specialization joins when the workload outgrows a node (dashed border) — not in the canonical baseline'. Only one of the three dashed boxes is explained by the caption; the other two are unexplained and semantically wrong under the caption's rule. Cross-check with printed page 191 (PDF 211), which describes PagedAttention/prefix caching as active mechanisms of the canonical 640 GB node baseline.
root_cause: The figure was authored with 'dashed = distinct/independent concern' (a stylistic device) while the caption repurposed 'dashed' as 'dashed = excluded from canonical baseline'. Two incompatible meanings were assigned to one visual channel.
correction: Pick one meaning for border style and make the figure and caption agree. Preferred: solid border for the three concerns present in the canonical baseline (1, 2, 3) and dashed for 4 only, plus a one-line legend inside the figure ('dashed = not in the canonical baseline; see § 11.3'). If the intended distinction was instead 'solid = scheduling, dashed = the other three', then rewrite the caption clause to say so explicitly and remove the '(dashed border)' parenthetical from the canonical-baseline sentence.
acceptance_test: Render the page and confirm: (a) exactly one box carries the 'not in canonical baseline' border style, and it is box 4; (b) a legend or caption clause states the border-style meaning unambiguously; (c) no reader can reach the conclusion 'PagedAttention and prefix caching are not in the canonical baseline' from the figure alone.

issue: The caption's central claim is that the four concerns 'interact — batching pressure feeds KV residency', and it gives a concrete coupling example ('prefix caching under aggressive continuous batching: cached prefixes and the live batch's pages draw on the same 640 GB KV pool, so reuse needs headroom'). The figure, however, draws four fully disconnected boxes with no arrows, no shared resource, and no coupling annotation. A reader who takes the diagram at face value learns 'four independent, non-interacting components' — which is the opposite of the caption's first clause and is the more consequential misconception, because the coupling (shared KV pool) is exactly what determines whether the four dials can be set independently in practice.
evidence: Rendered page 212: no connectors of any kind between boxes 1–4; the only shared object mentioned in the caption (the 640 GB KV pool) appears nowhere in the drawing. Title 'Serving = four separate concerns, not a stack' reinforces the 'independent' reading.
root_cause: The figure was designed to make the 'not a stack' point (no vertical ordering) and over-corrected into 'no relations at all', losing the interaction the caption asserts.
correction: Add a minimal interaction cue without implying a stack: e.g. a single dashed, non-directional connector or a shared '640 GB KV pool' band beneath boxes 2 and 3 labelled 'shared KV pool → reuse needs headroom', plus a small annotation on the 1→2 edge ('batching pressure → KV residency'). Keep the boxes unordered (no arrows forming a chain). Alternatively, retitle to 'Serving = four concerns, not a stack — but they interact' and let the caption carry the coupling.
acceptance_test: A reader shown only the figure (caption hidden) can state both (a) that the four concerns are not ordered as a stack and (b) that at least one pair shares a constrained resource and therefore cannot be tuned fully independently.

issue: Grayscale distinguishability is weak. The four boxes use hue alone to differentiate the concerns: purple (1), red (2), green (3), orange (4). In grayscale, red and orange collapse to nearly the same mid-gray, and green to a similar mid-gray; the only non-color differentiator is border style, which — per FIG-11.2-01 — is itself ambiguous and identical for boxes 2, 3 and 4. The italic 'e.g.' sub-labels are drawn in light tints of the same hues (light red, light green, light orange), which lose further contrast in grayscale and at the small size used. The book must remain interpretable in grayscale and for color-vision-deficient readers.
evidence: Rendered page 212 at 150 dpi: boxes 2/3/4 are visually near-identical in stroke weight and dash pattern, differing only by hue; the sub-label text is noticeably lower-contrast than the box titles.
root_cause: Color was used as the primary categorical channel with no redundant (shape/pattern/label) encoding, and the one redundant channel available (border style) was overloaded with a conflicting meaning.
correction: Add a redundant non-color channel: distinct border patterns per concern (solid / long-dash / dotted / double-line) or a small numeral badge plus a short axis label, and darken the 'e.g.' sub-labels to the same hue as their box titles (or to a neutral dark gray). Keep hue as a tertiary cue only.
acceptance_test: Convert the page to grayscale and confirm all four boxes remain individually identifiable by a non-color cue, and that every 'e.g.' sub-label remains legible at 100% print size.

issue: Two small semantic/pedagogical points. (a) The boxes are numbered 1–4 in reading order, which implies a sequence or precedence even though the title and caption insist the concerns are 'not a stack' and are addressed 'in any order'; the numbering is the only element in the drawing that suggests ordering. (b) The caption's closing italic paragraph states the actual intellectual payload — 'request scheduling exchanges latency for utilization, state management exchanges memory capacity for concurrency, reuse avoids re-prefill FLOPs, and resource specialization splits two compute/memory regimes into two pools' — but none of these trade-offs is encoded in the figure, so the figure carries the least informative content of the pair.
evidence: Rendered page 212: numerals '1 ·', '2 ·', '3 ·', '4 ·' precede the box titles; no trade-off text appears inside any box.
root_cause: Numbering was used for reference convenience; the trade-off dimension was left entirely to the caption.
correction: Either drop the numerals (or replace them with non-ordinal tags such as 'SCHED'/'STATE'/'REUSE'/'SPEC') so no ordering is implied, or add a one-line trade-off under each 'e.g.' label (e.g. 'latency ↔ utilization'). If the trade-offs are added, the figure becomes the primary carrier of the caption's key insight and the caption can be shortened.
acceptance_test: Figure alone conveys, for each of the four concerns, the mechanism and the resource it trades; no visual element implies an ordering among the four.

issue: Page composition: the figure plus its long caption (roughly 20 lines, including a separate italic paragraph) ends about three-quarters of the way down the page, leaving a large empty band at the bottom of a page that is otherwise a single figure-and-caption unit. The caption is also unusually long relative to the figure it annotates — the figure is four boxes with short labels, while the caption carries the mechanism choices, the interaction example, the canonical-baseline rule, the cross-reference to § 11.3, and a separate trade-off paragraph.
evidence: Rendered page 212: bottom ~25% of the text block is blank; caption occupies more vertical space than the diagram.
root_cause: Caption was written to stand alone as a mini-essay, and the figure was not sized to carry more of that content.
correction: Move the trade-off content into the figure (see FIG-11.2-04) and compress the caption to: what the figure shows, the canonical-baseline rule, and the § 11.3 pointer. This both shortens the caption and lets the figure be enlarged to fill the page, improving label legibility.
acceptance_test: Caption reduced to ≤ 12 lines; figure enlarged so that the smallest label is ≥ 8 pt at final print size; no page in the chapter ends with more than ~20% trailing whitespace.

figure: FIGURE 11.3 — P/D disaggregation: two cases, two different KV links
issue: Case A's KV volume is internally inconsistent: the byte/time annotation reads '~35 GB ≈ 0.08 s (on-node, undirectional)' but the workload annotation directly beneath it reads 'illustrative 1.3K-token, FP16 full-MHA'. At the book's canonical FP16 full-MHA KV rate (~2.62 MB/token), 1.3K tokens is ~3.4 GB, not 35 GB; 35 GB corresponds to ~13.3K tokens, which is exactly what case B states. Either case A's token count is wrong (should be 13.3K-token), or case A's byte/time figures are wrong (should be ~3.5 GB ≈ 0.008 s). As drawn, the figure's central comparison ('0.08 s vs 0.9 s') is either wrong or confounded by a 10× difference in workload, which contradicts the figure's own subtitle ('the P/D split is the same; the transfer link — and its cost — is not').
evidence: Figure text: A = '~35 GB ≈ 0.08 s (on-node, undirectional)' / 'illustrative 1.3K-token, FP16 full-MHA'; B = '~35 GB ≈ 0.9 s (cross-host)' / 'illustrative 13.3K-token, FP16 full-MHA'. Figure note: 'A: 0.08 s ≈ whole 35 GB over one unsharded 450 GB/s link (conservative; shard = 0.02 s).' Arithmetic: 35 GB ÷ 2.62 MB/token = 13,359 tokens ≈ 13.3K (matches B); 1.3K × 2.62 MB = 3.4 GB (does not match A's 35 GB). Time check: 35 GB ÷ 450 GB/s = 0.0778 s ≈ 0.08 s (so the 35 GB / 0.08 s pair is self-consistent and the token count is the outlier).
acceptance_test: At 100% zoom, read the case-A workload annotation. If it reads '1.3K-token', change it to '13.3K-token' (or change A's byte/time pair to '~3.5 GB ≈ 0.008 s' and re-derive the note). Acceptance: the identity 'bytes ÷ 2.62 MB/token = stated token count' holds for BOTH cases, and the two cases carry the same KV volume so that the only variable is the link.

figure: FIGURE 11.3 caption (prose claims) vs figure annotations
issue: The caption's numeric chain cannot be reconciled under a single prompt length and a single time base. The caption states 'per-request 1→19 PFLOPs over the ~1.08 s prefix budget vs 0.89 peak single-H100; on the canonical 8-H100 host the same prefix takes ~0.47 s at 35% MFU, Ch 12'. Two problems: (a) the FLOPs string is either '1.29 PFLOPs' (a low-resolution '1.29' can read as '1→19') or a literal range '1→19 PFLOPs' — if it is the latter it is wrong by ~15× for the canonical prefix; (b) '0.89 peak single-H100' equals 989 TFLOPS × 0.9 s, i.e. it is computed over 0.9 s while the comparison is stated against a '~1.08 s prefix budget' (peak over 1.08 s would be 1.07 PFLOPs). The two time bases are mixed in the same comparison. Separately, 'the same prefix takes ~0.47 s' is only consistent with ~1.29 PFLOPs (≈9.2K tokens), NOT with the figure's illustrative 13.3K-token prompt (≈1.86 PFLOPs → ≈0.67 s at 35% MFU on 8×H100), so 'the same prefix' is ambiguous between the canonical prefix and the figure's prompt.
evidence: Caption text as printed. Recomputation: 2·N_params·N_tokens for 70B at 9,200 tokens = 1.29 PFLOPs; 8 × 989 TFLOPS × 0.35 = 2.769 PFLOPS effective → 1.29 / 2.769 = 0.466 s ≈ 0.47 s (consistent). For 13.3K tokens: 1.86 PFLOPs → 0.672 s (not 0.47 s). 989 TFLOPS × 0.9 s = 0.89 PFLOPs; 989 TFLOPS × 1.08 s = 1.07 PFLOPs. Figure annotation: 'illustrative 13.3K-token'.
acceptance_test: Rewrite the caption so that (i) the prompt length is stated in tokens, (ii) the FLOPs figure is written unambiguously (e.g. '≈1.29 PFLOPs = 2·N·T for 9.2K tokens'), and (iii) the time base for '0.89 PFLOPs' is stated (e.g. '989 TFLOPS × 0.9 s of the 1.08 s budget'). Acceptance: a reader can reproduce 1.29 PFLOPs, 0.89 PFLOPs, and 0.47 s from the stated inputs, and the caption says explicitly whether 'the same prefix' is the canonical 9.2K-token prefix or the figure's 13.3K-token illustrative prompt.

issue: The bottom annotation row is semantically incoherent and contradicts the figure's stated thesis. Case A's prefill stage is fed by a label 'prompt' (up-arrow), while case B's prefill stage is fed by 'generated tokens → prompt' (up-arrow) — the two cases therefore show different inputs for the same stage, even though the subtitle asserts 'the P/D split is the same'. The label 'generated tokens → prompt' also mixes two arrow directions (a right-pointing '→' inside a label attached to an up-pointing arrow) and is not explained anywhere on the page: it is either an unexplained second-turn/feedback flow (which is not drawn as a distinct path) or a mislabeled arrow. The reader cannot tell which.
evidence: Figure bottom row, left to right: 'prompt' (up-arrow into case-A PREFILL); 'generated tokens →' (down-arrow from case-A DECODE); 'generated tokens → prompt' (up-arrow into case-B PREFILL); 'generated tokens →' (down-arrow from case-B DECODE). Subtitle: 'the P/D split is the same; the transfer link — and its cost — is not'. No prose on the page explains the 'generated tokens → prompt' label.
acceptance_test: Either (a) make both cases' prefill input 'prompt' and delete 'generated tokens → prompt', or (b) if a multi-turn feedback flow is intended, draw it as a visually distinct dashed path from the decode output back to the prefill input and add one clause of prose naming it. Acceptance: every arrow in the figure has exactly one label, and the two cases differ only in the link (and host boundary), never in the request flow.

figure: FIGURE 11.3 — headline transfer times vs figure note
issue: The headline per-case transfer times are the non-physical variant, while the physically realizable variant appears only in the smallest type in the note. The headline says '≈ 0.08 s (on-node, undirectional)' for 35 GB over one 450 GB/s link; the note says 'conservative; shard = 0.02 s'. With a 4-GPU tensor-parallel prefill stage, no single GPU holds the whole KV, so the unsharded 35 GB hop cannot occur — the realizable figure is 8.75 GB per GPU at 450 GB/s = 0.019 s. The figure therefore headlines an upper bound that is 4× the realizable value, and the reader is never told which number governs the decision the caption claims the figure informs ('the KV-transfer cost decides'). The on-node-vs-fabric ratio is either 11× (headline) or 45× (realizable) — a 4× difference in the figure's headline conclusion.
evidence: Figure headline: '~35 GB ≈ 0.08 s (on-node, undirectional)'. Figure note: 'A: 0.08 s ≈ whole 35 GB over one unsharded 450 GB/s link (conservative; shard = 0.02 s).' Recomputation: 35/4 = 8.75 GB; 8.75/450 = 0.0194 s ≈ 0.02 s; 0.875/0.0194 = 45× vs 0.875/0.0778 = 11×.
acceptance_test: Either headline the sharded (realizable) time and put the unsharded value in the note as an upper bound, or label the headline explicitly 'upper bound (unsharded)'. Acceptance: the figure states which number is used for the on-node-vs-fabric comparison, and the ratio quoted in the caption/prose matches that number.

figure: FIGURE 11.3 — host-boundary encoding, case A vs case B
issue: The visual device that encodes 'host' is inconsistent between the two cases, which undercuts the figure's central contrast (one NVLink domain vs across hosts). Case A's two stage boxes sit inside a single light-gray enclosure labelled '8× H100 host' at the top, so the reader sees that both stages share one host. Case B has no equivalent enclosure: '8× H100 host' appears as a line of text inside each colored stage box, so the reader must infer the host boundary from text. The second line of each stage box also carries different semantics in the two cases ('4 GPUs' in A, '8× H100 host' in B), so the same slot means 'GPU count' on the left and 'host descriptor' on the right.
evidence: Case A: light-gray rounded enclosure spanning both PREFILL and DECODE boxes with '8× H100 host' centred above them; inner boxes labelled 'PREFILL / 4 GPUs' and 'DECODE / 4 GPUs'. Case B: no enclosure; boxes labelled 'PREFILL / 8× H100 host' and 'DECODE / 8× H100 host'. Header: 'A. Within one NVLink domain (8 GPUs: 4+4). B. Across hosts (fabric)'.
acceptance_test: Apply the same host-boundary device in both cases (e.g. a light-gray enclosure around each host, with the fabric link drawn crossing between two enclosures), and make the second line of every stage box mean the same thing (GPU count). Acceptance: a reader can state, from the geometry alone, that case A's stages share one host and case B's do not.

issue: The two KV links — the entire subject of the figure — are drawn identically: both are solid red right-pointing arrows with a red 'KV' label above and a red bandwidth label below. Nothing in the drawing distinguishes an on-node NVLink hop from a cross-host fabric hop except the position of the boxes and the text of the bandwidth label. In grayscale (and for a color-vision-deficient reader) the two links are indistinguishable, so the figure's title claim ('two different KV links') is carried entirely by words rather than by the visual encoding. A line-style or fill distinction (solid = NVLink, dashed = fabric) would carry the distinction in grayscale and would also make the 'sharded vs unsharded' distinction in the note visible.
evidence: Case A: solid red arrow, 'KV' above, '450 GB/s per GPU per direction' below. Case B: solid red arrow, 'KV' above, '40 GB/s per host NIC' below. Both arrows are the same color, weight, and style.
acceptance_test: Differentiate the two links by line style (and, if useful, by arrowhead or a small link glyph) in addition to color, and confirm the distinction survives a grayscale conversion. Acceptance: a grayscale rendering of the page still lets the reader tell which hop is on-node and which is cross-host without reading the bandwidth labels.

issue: The smallest in-figure annotations appear to be set below the 8 pt floor used for figure annotations and body prose: the two 'illustrative …, FP16 full-MHA' lines, the '450 GB/s per GPU per direction' and '40 GB/s per host NIC' labels, the 'square = one GPU (hatched = prefill)' legend, and the four-line note block ('Caveat — aggregate KV migration at peak…'). By relative glyph height against the caption body text, these sit at roughly 65–75% of body size (≈6.5–7.5 pt). This is compounded by information design: the decisive caveats (the 'shard = 0.02 s' alternative and the '1.4 TB/s exceeds any single link' conclusion) live only in the smallest type at the bottom of the figure. The figure currently occupies about 85% of the text-block width and less than half of the available vertical space, so there is room to enlarge it by roughly 15–20% without collision.
evidence: Rendered page 213: the note block's line 'A: 0.08 s ≈ whole 35 GB over one unsharded 450 GB/s link (conservative; shard = 0.02 s).' is visibly much smaller than the caption body text directly below the figure; the same holds for the 'illustrative …' lines and the legend. The figure's bounding box ends roughly 30 px above the caption, leaving unused vertical space.
acceptance_test: Measure the smallest glyph height in the figure source at 100% zoom and confirm ≥ 8 pt; if below, scale the figure up (or promote the note block to body-size text) until it is. Acceptance: no in-figure annotation is below 8 pt, and the note block is legible at 100% on a printed proof without magnification.

issue: Red carries two unrelated meanings in this figure: it outlines the PREFILL stage box (stage identity) and it draws the KV transfer arrow plus the KV bandwidth labels (data-path identity). In grayscale, red and orange (the prefill GPU tiles) also converge in luminance, so the prefill box outline, the prefill tiles, and the KV path all fall into a similar tone band. Shape carries most of the load, so the figure is still readable, but the visual language is not doing the work it appears to do.
evidence: Case A/B: PREFILL box outline red; KV arrow red; 'KV', '450 GB/s per GPU per direction', '40 GB/s per host NIC' red; prefill GPU tiles orange with diagonal hatch; decode box outline and tiles blue. Grayscale luminance of red and orange are close.
acceptance_test: Reserve one hue for stage identity (orange = prefill, blue = decode) and render the KV path in a neutral/dark tone with a distinct line style. Acceptance: in grayscale, no two semantically different elements share both hue and shape.

issue: The figure is labeled '[ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED]' as a whole, but it mixes three provenance classes: the 450 GB/s per-GPU-per-direction NVLink figure is a first-party hardware specification, the 40 GB/s per-host NIC figure is an assumption about the fabric, and the 13.3K-token prompt is an illustrative workload. A single trailing label on the figure under-covers the hardware and assumption spans, so a reader cannot tell which numbers are measured hardware facts and which are chosen for the illustration.
evidence: Caption: 'FIGURE 11.3: P/D disaggregation has two cases, two KV links; the KV-transfer cost decides — see Note 1.3-1. [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED]'. Figure contents: '450 GB/s per GPU per direction' (H100 NVLink spec), '40 GB/s per host NIC' (assumed fabric), 'illustrative 13.3K-token' (illustrative workload).
acceptance_test: Split the label span so that the hardware-specification and assumption numbers carry their own markers (e.g. [1P] on the 450 GB/s label, [ASSUMPTION] on the 40 GB/s label), or state the provenance of each in the caption. Acceptance: every number in the figure can be assigned to exactly one provenance class by the reader.

issue: The caveat's aggregate figure uses '40 req/s' — a canonical-workload rate — with no attribution inside the figure, so the reader cannot tell whether it is the book's canonical request rate or an illustrative peak. This matters because the caveat's whole point is a peak-aggregate argument: if 40 req/s is canonical, the 1.4 TB/s figure is a canonical-workload result and should be labeled as such; if it is illustrative, the caveat should say so.
evidence: Figure note: 'Caveat — aggregate KV migration at peak: 35 GB/request × 40 req/s = 1.4 TB/s of payload.' The caption points to 'Note 1.3-1' for the canonical numbers but the figure itself carries no pointer.
acceptance_test: Add '(canonical)' or '(illustrative)' to the 40 req/s figure, or add an in-figure pointer to Note 1.3-1. Acceptance: the reader can determine the provenance of 40 req/s from the figure alone.

figure: FIGURE 11.3 — case headers and legend placement
issue: Two small layout issues. (a) The two case headers are run together on a single line as one sentence — 'A. Within one NVLink domain (8 GPUs: 4+4). B. Across hosts (fabric)' — so the reader's eye must split one line into two headers, and the period after '(8 GPUs: 4+4)' reads as sentence punctuation rather than as a header boundary. (b) The legend 'square = one GPU (hatched = prefill)' is placed inside the case-A panel, where it can be read as applying only to case A, although it governs the GPU tiles in both cases.
evidence: Rendered page 213: single header line spanning both cases; legend text sits at the lower-left inside the case-A enclosure, well away from the case-B tiles.
acceptance_test: Set each case header on its own line directly above its case, and move the legend to a position that reads as figure-wide (e.g. below both cases, or immediately under the figure title). Acceptance: each header is visually bound to one case, and the legend's scope is unambiguous.

issue: The note's parenthetical '(per-GPU in a per-host NIC in B)' is grammatically and semantically ambiguous: it can be read as 'per-GPU [link] in A, per-host NIC in B' or as 'per-GPU [traffic] carried over a per-host NIC in B'. The two readings imply different link-sharing assumptions, and the second reading would change the 35 GB ÷ 40 GB/s = 0.875 s figure.
evidence: Figure note: 'Per-request times assume an unsharded dedicated link (per-GPU in a per-host NIC in B).'
acceptance_test: Rewrite as an unambiguous sentence, e.g. 'Per-request times assume a dedicated link: per-GPU NVLink in A, one per-host NIC in B.' Acceptance: the link-sharing assumption for each case is stated in one unambiguous clause.
